bundle.author: jagoda
bundle.title: Stop a task replacement from emptying the gateway for seven minutes
bundle.body:
The gateway is up now, but every workbench apply empties it for about seven and a half minutes. This shortens that to roughly one to two, and states what the rest would cost.

## What happened

`https://bifrost.workbench.goodparty.org/health` was 503 from **21:27:36Z** to **21:35:13Z** on 2026-10-26, across #377's apply. Verified from the ECS logs and the deploy run, not inferred from the symptom:

| time (Z) | event |
|---|---|
| 21:27:36 | apply finishes; ECS deregisters the only task |
| 21:29–21:33 | ALB 503 on `/health` and `/` (probed) |
| 21:33:16 | old task (`1562504153`) logs its last line, "🏁 server stopped" |
| 21:34:21 | replacement (`91cc7e1b`) starts |
| 21:34:44 | "successfully started bifrost"; **"Time spent in Bifrost server bootstrap 23163 ms"** (store migrations) |
| 21:35:13 | 503 → 200 |

Nothing failed. The replacement started, booted and passed its health check; the outage was the shape of the replacement, and almost all of it was two defaults:

1. **Deregistration delay 300s.** The service is stop-before-start (`ecs.ts:133-134`), so ECS takes the only target out of the target group immediately and *then* waits out the delay before stopping the task. That 300 seconds is a hard outage, not a drain window that keeps traffic flowing.
2. **Health check timing.** `interval: 30`, `healthyThreshold: 3` (provider defaults) — another 60 to 90 seconds after the process is answering before the ALB will send it traffic.

## What changes

- `ingress.ts`: the target groups pin `deregistrationDelay: 30` and `interval: 10`, `timeout: 5`, `healthyThreshold: 2`, `unhealthyThreshold: 3`, as named constants, so the outage shape is a reviewable diff rather than a provider default that moves.
- `ecs.ts`: the container health check's `startPeriod` goes from 30s to 90s. The measured first boot is 23.1s; 30 seconds of start period leaves about seven seconds of margin before a slow boot is reported unhealthy, and a task that is slow because it is migrating should not be restarted.

Expected gap after this: ~30s deregistration + task stop + Fargate launch + ~25s boot + ~20s of health checks, so one to two minutes instead of seven and a half.

## What this deliberately does not do

The gap is not zero, and the change that would make it zero is a rolling update (`minimumHealthyPercent: 100`, `maximumPercent: 200`), which runs two Bifrost instances at once. `ecs.ts:112-131` explains why that is not the current shape: OSS Bifrost is single-node, keeps governance state in memory, and runs store migrations at startup, so the pair could race the schema. Making that call needs a migration-concurrency answer (advisory lock or a one-shot migration task) — a decision for the reviewer, not something to slip into a timing fix.

The 30-second deregistration delay does truncate an in-flight streaming response that outlives it. That is the trade while the endpoint serves no production traffic; when a harness depends on it, revisit the delay and the rolling decision together.

## Verification

`npx tsc --noEmit` clean. `npm test`: **694 tests, 134 suites, 0 fail**. The new ingress test pins every value above and asserts the resource actually sets them; the ecs test now asserts `startPeriod === 90` instead of `>= 15`.

Not verified: the post-change gap, which needs an apply. `WorkbenchAccess` here cannot read ECS service state (`ecs:DescribeServices` denied) or target health, so the pre-change timeline above is reconstructed from CloudWatch logs, the deploy run, and live probing; the post-change number comes from the first deploy after this merges.

Related: #378 fixes the preflight crash that currently blocks every workbench apply, so it has to land before this can be observed in a deploy. Closing #371 was part of the same investigation; it was superseded by #377.

---
> Brought to you by in silico Jeff (pi, deepseek-v4p1-flash-1017)

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes ALB target-group drain and health timing plus ECS container start grace—directly affects every deploy’s availability window and long-lived streams during replacement, though behavior is intentional and test-pinned.
> 
> **Overview**
> Workbench applies were leaving the Bifrost gateway **503 for ~7½ minutes** on every task replacement—not a failed deploy, but stop-before-start plus ALB defaults (300s deregistration delay and slow health-check promotion).
> 
> **`ingress.ts`** pins both target groups to **30s deregistration** and **10s health checks** (2 healthy / 3 unhealthy), exported as named constants so outage shape stays reviewable. **`ecs.ts`** raises the gateway container ECS **`startPeriod` from 30s to 90s** so boots that run store migrations (~23s measured) are not killed as unhealthy mid-migration. Comments in `ecs.ts` tie the long gap to ingress timing and note that zero-downtime would need rolling deploys and a migration-concurrency story.
> 
> Tests assert the exact pinned values and that `ingress.ts` wires them on every target group.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit c54f9b8cbc20edebbf492d4b255c77bc35df3df0. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>
<!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

findings.body:
**A slow migrating boot can now be killed by the ALB check, which `startPeriod` does not cover.** The target group now marks a target unhealthy after 3 failures at 10s intervals, about 30s after ECS registers it. The ECS service in `ecs.ts` (around line 1160, `loadBalancers: [...]`) sets no `healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds`, so it uses the default of 0. With no grace period, ECS replaces a task as soon as its ELB target goes unhealthy. The container `startPeriod` raised to 90s in this PR only applies to the container-level check, not the ELB one.

The measured first boot is 23.1s, and that is not counting registration and sidecar timing. That leaves about the same ~7s margin the PR description calls too thin for the container check. The old defaults (30s × 3) allowed about 90s. A migration that runs a little slower would get the task marked unhealthy and replaced. The replacement then runs the same migration again, so the service could loop through restarts while staying stop-before-start with one task.

The fix is to set `healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds` on the service to at least `BIFROST_HEALTH_CHECK.startPeriod`. That keeps the faster promotion and still protects a booting task.

Falsification check: this is wrong if the service sets `healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds` anywhere. Grepping `deploy-workbench/` for `healthCheckGracePeriod` returns no matches.

output.summary: The diff matches the PR description. In `ingress.ts`, both target groups now pin deregistration delay to 30s and health checks to a 10s interval, 5s timeout and 2/3 thresholds, set through named constants inside the per-group map. In `ecs.ts`, the gateway container's `startPeriod` goes from 30s to 90s, and the tests assert the exact values. The scout flagged three areas. Two test leads were ruled out: the settings are applied inside the map over `TARGET_GROUPS`, so every group gets them, and the oauth2-proxy container has no container health check that would need the same change. The third lead held up: the ALB timing now fails a booting target about 30s after registration, and the ECS service has no health-check grace period to protect a task that is still migrating. That interaction is left as an inline comment. A human should confirm the real gap after the first deploy, and confirm migration duration against a non-empty store, since neither can be checked from code.
